strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/s: Spanish is read almost as it is written
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/0/p: There are only five vowels and they always sound the same: a, e, i, o, u. They are short and clear.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/1/h: C and G change before e, i
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/1/p: Before e or i, c sounds like English "th" (in Spain) and g sounds like a strong h. Before a, o, u they sound k and g.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/2/p: H is silent. Ll sounds like "y". Ñ sounds "ny". J sounds like a strong h. Z sounds like "th".
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/3/p: The rr (and r at the start) is a rolled sound. It changes the meaning: pero and perro are different words.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/sec/4/p: The accent mark shows the stressed syllable. Without one, words ending in a vowel, n or s are stressed on the second-to-last syllable.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/q/0/3: The h is silent in Spanish.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/0/q/1/3: Before e or i, c sounds like "th" in Spain.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/1/s: el, la, los, las and un, una, unos, unas
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/1/sec/0/p: The article depends on the gender and number of the noun.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/1/sec/1/p: Un (masculine), una (feminine), unos and unas in the plural. Careful: el agua, un águila (feminine, but with el / un because of the sound).
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/1/q/0/3: Amigo is masculine singular: el amigo.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/1/q/2/3: Libros is masculine plural: los libros.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/2/sec/0/p: Most nouns ending in -o are masculine, in -a feminine. Nouns in -e can be either, so learn them one by one.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/2/sec/1/p: Vowel + s: gato, gatos. Consonant + es: ciudad, ciudades.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/2/sec/2/p: If it ends in -z, the plural is -ces: lápiz, lápices. Some words do not change: el lunes, los lunes.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/2/q/1/3: The z changes to c: lápices.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/3/sec/0/p: Remove -ar, -er or -ir and add the ending for each person.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/3/sec/1/p: Since the ending already says who it is, the pronoun is usually left out.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/3/sec/1/ex/1/1: I speak Spanish, he speaks French.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/3/sec/2/p: Some change the stem vowel: quiero, puedo, pido. They do not change with nosotros and vosotros.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/4/sec/0/p: Ser is for identity, origin, profession, nationality and time.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/4/sec/1/p: Estar is for states (tired, happy) and for saying where something is.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/4/sec/2/p: With some adjectives, ser and estar give different meanings.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/5/sec/0/p: In Spanish questions have ¿ at the start and ? at the end. Word order barely changes: only the intonation rises.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/5/sec/1/p: They all carry an accent mark.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/5/sec/2/p: "Por qué" (two words, with accent) asks. "Porque" (one word) answers.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/6/sec/0/p: Put no right before the verb.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/6/sec/1/p: If the negative word comes after the verb, you also need no: no veo a nadie.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/6/q/0/0: I want to say "I do not speak"
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/7/s: a, de, en, con, por, para
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/7/sec/0/p: A = direction. De = origin or possession. En = place. Con = company.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/7/sec/1/p: a + el = al. de + el = del. They do not merge with la, los or las.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/7/sec/2/p: Para = purpose or destination. Por = cause, time or passing through.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/8/sec/0/p: They change with gender and number: alto, alta, altos, altas.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/8/sec/1/p: They do not change with gender: grande, fácil, joven. They only take -s or -es in the plural.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/8/sec/2/p: They almost always go after the noun. A few short ones go before and shorten: buen amigo, gran ciudad.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/8/q/2/3: Bueno shortens before a masculine noun: buen amigo.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/9/sec/0/p: You have to learn them by heart.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/9/sec/1/p: From 16 to 29 they are one word: dieciséis, veintiuno. From 31 they are separate: treinta y uno.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/9/sec/2/p: Cien becomes ciento before another number: ciento uno. Mil does not change: dos mil.
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/9/q/0/3: From 31 it is written separately with "y".
strings.modules/TOPICS#1/9/q/2/3: Mil stays the same in the plural.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/0/sec/0/p: Haber in the present + participle. Participle: -ar → -ado, -er/-ir → -ido.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/0/sec/1/p: Some do not follow the rule: hecho, dicho, visto, escrito, puesto, abierto, vuelto, roto.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/0/sec/2/p: In Spain it is used for the recent past or what is still linked to today: today, this week, already, not yet.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/0/sec/2/ex/0/1: Today I have worked a lot.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/1/sec/0/p: They go before the conjugated verb: me, te, se, nos, os, se.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/1/sec/1/p: Many routine verbs are reflexive: despertarse, ducharse, vestirse, acostarse.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/2/sec/0/p: The thing you like is the subject. Me gusta el café = the coffee pleases me. With plurals: me gustan los gatos.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/2/sec/1/p: Encantar, interesar, doler and parecer work the same way.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/3/sec/0/p: The first verb is conjugated and the second stays in the infinitive.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/3/sec/1/p: Tener que + infinitive = obligation. Ir a + infinitive = plan.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/3/sec/1/ex/1/1: I am going to travel tomorrow.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/3/sec/2/p: Quisiera and ¿podría...? sound more polite than quiero and ¿puedes...?
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#1/3/sec/2/ex/0/1: I would like a coffee, please.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/sec/0/p: Add to the whole infinitive: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án. It is the same for -ar, -er and -ir.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/sec/1/p: They change the stem: tener → tendré, poder → podré, hacer → haré, decir → diré, salir → saldré, venir → vendré.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/sec/2/p: In conversation ir a + infinitive is very common.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/0/sec/2/ex/0/1: I am going to call you.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/1/s: mi, tu, su; este, ese, aquel
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/1/sec/0/p: They go before the noun and agree with the thing owned: mi libro, mis libros, nuestra casa.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/1/sec/1/p: Este (here), ese (near you), aquel (far). They change in gender and number.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/1/q/0/3: Mi goes with a singular noun.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/2/sec/0/p: It is the same as the he-form: habla, come, escribe.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/2/sec/1/p: The vowel changes: -ar → -e, -er/-ir → -a. Hable, coma, escriba.
strings.modules/TOPICS.push#2/2/sec/2/p: To forbid, use no + subjunctive: no hables, no comas.
